Issue: [#2042](https://github.com/openagt/openagent/issues/2042)

# A comment on an agent's pull request resumes that agent

## TLDR

Today a comment on a pull request an agent opened starts a new agent, which knows nothing of the first one's conversation. Instead:

1. **The comment resumes the run that opened the pull request.** The scheduler finds new comments, looks up the run whose record names that pull request, and resumes it with the comments handed over.
2. **The resumed agent reads the thread again first**, and answers from the thread as it stands.
3. **Fallback when the run cannot be resumed here** (it ran on another machine, or its conversation is gone): a new agent starts, told to read the first agent's record and the thread first.
4. **One agent per pull request**: a comment never reaches two agents.
5. **A row on the Automations page**, off by default like every row, with its pace and its publish level.

Not part of this: GitHub calling the machine when a comment arrives (the scheduler asks, as every row does); a session that stays alive between comments.

## Why it matters

The agent that wrote the code knows why it is so, what was tried and dropped, and what was promised on the thread; a fresh agent does not. Every run's record already keeps its pull request, and runs can already be resumed: nothing connects the two yet.

## Open questions

1. Whose comments count: anyone's, or only people who can write to the repository. The agent's own comments must never count.
2. Line review comments and failing checks: the same way, or later.
3. A pull request a person opened, with no run behind it: nothing, or a new agent.
4. Which machine: only the one that ran the first agent holds its conversation.

## Notes

- https://github.com/nitedani/mergeworthy works this way ("the session is the agent"): a watcher per thread only records events and adds 👀; the session that opened the pull request is woken and drafts its answer from one file holding the whole thread and the threads it links to.

Work one task off the project's agent queue. Nobody will answer you: never ask, decide yourself.

Take the first open entry of the queue, and one task only. An entry `Create tickets/<name>.plan.md` names the ticket `tickets/<name>.md`. When the entry names a ticket, claim the ticket before you work it; when someone else holds the claim, leave that entry and take the next one; when every entry is claimed, say so and stop. When the entry's ticket no longer exists, mark the entry done and stop.

If the ticket is waiting or in review, do nothing on it, not even a plan: mark the queue entry done, release your claim and stop. If you find the ticket has nothing you can do until something outside the work happens, write what it waits on as its `Waiting:` line above the title, mark the entry done and release your claim. Never close a waiting ticket.

Commit your work on your branch. Once it is committed, publish it as far as whoever started you said; when they said nothing, publish nothing. If the push or the pull request fails, leave the entry queued, release your claim, and end saying what failed.

A task that opens no pull request ends when what it writes is saved where it belongs, then its queue entry is marked done. A plan is written as the ticket's plan: release your claim, the ticket stays open. A task whose whole work is changing other tickets finishes its own ticket: close it.

If this project has no AI queue, or the task needs a ticketing system or a way to open a pull request that the project lacks, end with an error saying so and stop.

I'm realizing the scheduler being per-machine creates ambiguity: since machine B can't know whether machine A still owns a run's conversation, it can't safely decide when to fall back and start a new agent for that run without risking duplication.

I'm settling on the simplest rule: only the machine that owns a run's host handles its comments — resuming if possible, or starting a fallback run there if the session is gone — and leaves runs owned by other hosts alone, leaving the "PR without a run" case out of scope for now. I also need to check how an active run receives new comments while working (likely via an inbox mechanism in parent.ts and the agent-runner CLI), and figure out how this fits into the scheduler's model of spawning new runs via markers, since resuming isn't a new spawn and doesn't fit neatly as a skill-based automations row.

I'm weighing two designs: option A spins up a dedicated `pr-comments` skill whose check surfaces new comments tagged with run ids, but that forces the scheduler to spawn a fresh run just to relay a resume, which feels wasteful. Option B instead extends the schedule's front matter with a `resumes: true` key so the check's JSON output of `{run, text}` pairs tells the scheduler to resume existing runs directly rather than spawning new ones, with the github skill's check calling out to map PR comments to their corresponding run ids since the last check.

But then I realize tracking "since when" gets messy -- normal lastStart logic won't count resumed runs, so I'm considering instead anchoring "new comments" to each run's own recorded endedAt timestamp, which is elegant per-PR but raises the question of whether comments posted during a resume's execution window would get missed on the next check.

I think the resolution is: trigger resuming only when a comment lands after the run's endedAt, but hand over everything since the run's last start, since the agent always re-reads the thread at the start anyway -- that way nothing slips through the gap between read and end.

For the fallback case where resuming isn't possible, a fresh run should spin up on the same row, inherit the earlier run's id plus pending comments, and keep working the same PR branch -- so its record also names the pull request, letting future comments resolve to whichever run most recently claimed that PR.

On the question of who counts, I'm leaning toward collaborators with write/maintain/admin access, but realize agent comments get posted under the human's own GitHub login rather than a distinct bot account, so author-based filtering won't separate agent comments from human ones. I need some kind of marker, like a signature line or hidden HTML comment tagging the run id, and should check how the github skill actually posts comments to see if this already exists.

For scope, I'll include line review comments and review bodies alongside issue comments since they're cheap to fetch, and leave failing checks for later. The Automations page rows come from skills themselves — the github skill would need schedule front matter to appear there automatically, off by default. Each run only affects its own host's scheduler, not others; if a host's row is off, nothing happens, and a host that's gone forever is out of scope for now. I want to check skill-github and the agent-runner's CLI to see how schedule front matter gets parsed.

# GitHub

The project's pull requests and issues are on GitHub. This skill is how you reach them.

## The command

Run the `github` command inside your checkout, always by its full name: `npx @openagt/skill-github@0.1`. It prints JSON; a refusal exits 1 with a line on stderr; a wrong command line exits 2 with the usage.

## Your pull request

Open a pull request only when your task or the person asks for one, or asks you to publish your work. Push your branch first (your branches skill says how), then:

```
npx @openagt/skill-github@0.1 open --title "<one line naming what the change does>" --body "<what changed, and why>"
```

It opens the pull request for the branch you are on and prints it in `request` (`number`, `url`). A branch that already has an open pull request gets no second one: that one is answered, with `existing` true. Add `--merge` when the work may land on its own: the pull request then merges once its checks pass, also where the repository does not allow auto-merge (`merge` in the answer says `auto-armed`, `merged` or `watching`). Add `--draft` instead for a pull request a person should look at first; with `--merge` too, `--draft` is dropped.

A pull request whose body has a line `Closes #<number>` closes that issue when it merges.

/**
 * A run started for another run, its parent (`run --parent <id>`), tells the parent when it ends:
 * one line saying which run, how it ended, and its last words. The line reaches the parent the way
 * a person's message reaches a run: into its inbox while it works, as a resume once it has ended.
 * Nothing waits for a child: the parent's agent ends its turn, and the line is its next prompt.
 */

/** How a run ended, as its parent is told. */
export interface ChildEnd {
  id: string
  status: string
  /** Why, when the run did not end well. */
  detail?: string
  /** The question the run stopped on, when it ended waiting. */
  question?: string
  /** The branch the run's work is on, when it still exists. */
  branch?: string
  pr?: { url: string }
  /** The agent's answer on its last turn. */
  lastWords?: string
}

/** The line a parent gets: which run, how it ended, where its work is, and its last words. */
export function childEndedLine(end: ChildEnd): string {
  const lines = [`The run ${end.id}, started for this run, ended ${end.status}${end.detail ? `: ${end.detail}` : ''}.`]
  if (end.question !== undefined) lines.push(`It is waiting on a question: ${end.question.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()}`)
  if (end.branch !== undefined) lines.push(`Its work is on the branch ${end.branch}.`)
  if (end.pr) lines.push(`Its pull request: ${end.pr.url}`)
  const words = end.lastWords?.trim()
  if (words) lines.push('', 'Its last words:', words)
  return lines.join('\n')
}

I'm considering adding `agent-runner tell <id> <text>` that generalizes the existing tellParent logic, writing to the inbox while the run is active or resuming once it's ended, while leaving the scheduler's gating logic for caps and quotas untouched.

Now I'm working through the fallback behavior: when a resumable run is for another machine's process, falling back to starting a new run risks creating duplicate agents if both machines act on the same PR. I'm leaning toward the rule that each host only handles runs it owns, and other hosts fall back to starting a fresh run with the attached text when the owning host's session appears missing.

For determining "since," I'll treat each run's endedAt timestamp as the cutoff, updated whenever a resume completes. For comment filtering, I'm planning a skill-github comment command that embeds a hidden marker so the check can skip its own agent-authored comments, plus skip bot comments and filter by author_association to only act on comments from users with write permission.

# [Plan] A comment on an agent's pull request resumes that agent

How a new comment on a pull request a run opened reaches that run instead of a new agent: the parts, the picks made for the ticket's open questions, and the order of the work.

## What is there already

- A run's record keeps its pull request (`pr` on the card, `packages/skill-logs/src/run.ts:39`), its host (`runnerMark(card).host`) and its coding agent's session (`caller.sessionId`).
- `agent-runner run --resume <id> <text>` continues an ended run in its session (`packages/agent-runner/src/run.ts:327`); a run still recorded running is refused.
- `tellParent` (`packages/agent-runner/src/parent.ts:63`) already hands one line to a run the right way either way: into its inbox while it works, as a resume once it has ended, with the race between the two closed. Only children use it today.
- The scheduler only starts new runs: a row's check prints JSON, and `decide` (`packages/agent-scheduler/src/tick.ts`) marks and spawns one run handed that output. Rows come from skills' `schedule` front matter; the tool names no skill.
- `#2138` settled that a run another computer started is only read here: continued here it would have none of its conversation.

## Picks for the open questions

1. **Whose comments count**: those whose `author_association` is `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or `COLLABORATOR` (GitHub puts it on every comment, no extra call), not a bot's (`user.type == "Bot"`), and never one an agent posted. Agents post under the person's own login, so the author cannot tell them apart: an agent's comment carries a hidden line `<!-- openagent-run: <id> -->`, and comments with it are skipped. Picked over anyone's (a stranger's comment would spend the person's quota) and over the author alone (the person and their agents share it).

## Considerations

- The agent's comments under the person's login are the sharpest edge: an agent that posts with `gh` directly, not the new command, would resume itself in a loop. Guard: skip comments whose `created_at` falls between the run's last start and its `endedAt` and whose author is the logged-in user (`gh api user`), as a second filter.
- A pull request merged or closed is not open: no tells. A run deleted from the records: its pull request has no run, nothing.
- The first tick after the row is switched on would hand every comment newer than each run's end; that is the point (comments nobody answered), but bounded to open pull requests.
- Rate limits: three `gh api` calls per open agent pull request per pace; at 10 minutes this is far under GitHub's limit.

## Implementation order

1. `agent-runner`: `tellRun` + `tell` command + tests (working run → inbox; ended → resume; other host / no session refused).
2. `skill-github`: `comment` command, `comments` check with its filter, tests with a fake `gh`; `SKILL.md` text and `schedule`.
3. `agent-scheduler`: `tells` key, `decide` branch, fallback, `listed`; tests in `tick.test.ts` and `schedule.test.ts`.
4. Automations page wording for a `tells` row (`AutomationsPage.tsx`), its test.

I wrote the plan for the first queue entry, **"A comment on an agent's pull request resumes that agent"** (#2042). It's saved as `tickets/2026-10-09_pr-comment-resumes-agent.plan.md` on `agent-data`. I've released my claim, the ticket stays open, and its queue entry is marked done. I didn't change anything on my code branch, so there was nothing to commit and nothing was published.

The plan rates it Effort 6 and Uncertainty 5. Main points:

- **How it works:** the github skill gets a scheduled check. It lists new comments on open pull requests opened by a run from this computer, and only once that run has ended. The scheduler then resumes that run with the comments, instead of starting a new agent. A skill turns this on with a new `tells: runs` key in its `schedule` front matter, so the scheduler itself still names no skill.
- **Fallback:** if the run can't be resumed because its conversation is gone, a new run starts. It's told to read the first run's record and the whole thread first, then work on the same branch.
- **Whose comments count:** the repository's owners, members and collaborators, never bots. An agent's comments go out under the person's own login, so agents post through a new `comment` command that adds a hidden marker. The check skips comments carrying it.
- **Review comments:** line comments and review bodies count the same way. Failing checks are left for a later ticket.
- **Pull requests without a run:** nothing happens.

**Decision for you:** the plan narrows one part of the ticket. Only the computer that ran the agent answers comments on its pull request. The ticket's fallback "it ran on another computer" is dropped, because if every computer with the row on answered, one comment could reach two agents, which the ticket rules out. The cost is that a run whose computer never switches the row on is never answered. The plan notes this pick, and it's the main reason for the uncertainty score.
